source.title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
source.authors: Zora Che; Stephen Casper; Robert Kirk; Anirudh Satheesh; Stewart Slocum; Lev McKinney; Rohit Gandikota; Aidan Ewart; Domenic Rosati; Zichu Wu; Zi-Kui Cai; Bilal Chughtai; Yarin Gal; Furong Huang; Dylan Hadfield-Menell

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites the original refusal-direction study but does not test or rely on that direction. Its refusal-model experiments evaluate general jailbreak and tampering attacks, without measuring whether they act by suppressing the direction.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response increases after attacks on refusal-tuned models (Figure 8), but does not identify, remove, add, or measure the single refusal direction. Those behavioral results are recorded under fits_no_version; they do not test the direction-specific mechanism in the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Arditi et al. (2024) only as an example of activation engineering. It never computes, ablates, adds or measures a difference-in-means refusal direction. Its jailbreak results (Figure 8) are attack success rates of input-space, latent, pruning and fine-tuning attacks on nine Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants, with no link to a refusal direction. The latent-space attack is a universal L2-bounded perturbation at layer 5, not a direction ablation. These results bear on none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the emphasis should be broader. The authors conclude that model tampering attacks, especially few-shot fine-tuning, conservatively exceed input-space attack success and can help predict it. Attack resilience lies on a low-dimensional subspace (3 PCs explain 89% of variance for unlearning, 96% for jailbreaking). Unlearning is undone within 16 fine-tuning steps. The jailbreaking setting gives similar results, except that no clear correlation appears between tampering and input-space attacks, with only 9 models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates varied jailbreak and model-tampering attacks, not the original difference-in-means direction or its ablation/addition procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports attack-method differences: fine-tuning and Cascade are particularly effective against refusal-tuned models. It also cautions that correlations between tampering and input-space attack success are unclear with only nine refusal-model samples.

fits_no_version.finding: All eight refusal-tuned Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants, including RR, LAT and TAR, showed increased harmful compliance under few-shot fine-tuning (up to 0.75–0.92 under Cascade) and under Cascade multi-turn attacks. Input-space attacks produced small increases (mostly ≤0.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal fine-tuning in Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants is easily undone by few-shot fine-tuning attacks, regardless of the robustness method, with no mechanism identified.

record.problems: The refusal-model study covers only nine Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants; the authors say this is too few to draw strong conclusions about correlations between tampering and input-space attacks. The direction-specific claim is not investigated.
record.rows_left_out: No direction-specific results are reported. Figure 8 contains per-model/per-attack harmful-response changes, but the recorded aggregate row captures the paper's explicit summary relevant to the broader behavior; no direction-specific version is tested.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction; no ablation or addition; no capability effect of such an intervention.
No direction-based weight edit or abliteration.
No analysis of whether attacks suppress a refusal direction; no training against direction ablation.
No refusal geometry studied. The PCA is over attack-success matrices across models, not activations.
Harm judgment and refusal are not separated.
No direction transfer across languages, variants or base to instruct models.
Refusal-training methods are compared only by attack vulnerability, not by whether a single removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: Classification as cites_only/T6 is confirmed. Arditi et al. appears only in the related-work list on activation engineering. The 'low-dimensional robustness subspace' concerns attack-success variation across models, not refusal representations, so it is not a V4 result.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is found or ablated or added; no general-capability effect of such an intervention is measured.
No direction-based ablation is converted into a weight edit or evaluated as abliteration.
The attacks are not tested for suppressing the refusal direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
No alternative refusal-direction geometry or multiplicity is tested.
The study does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or training stages is tested.
No experiment tests how refusal-training choices determine whether a single removable direction exists.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct refusal-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Applied input-space and model-tampering jailbreak attacks and measured increases in harmful responses; the text highlights fine-tuning and Cascade attacks.

conditions.value: refusal/safety-tuned Llama-3-8B-Instruct variants; aggregate result stated for all safety-tuning methods
attacks shown in Figure 8; authors specifically highlight fine-tuning and Cascade

rows.measure: Increase in harmful response rate after attack
rows.baseline: Direct harmful-request compliance baseline is shown in Figure 8; numeric baseline not stated in the accompanying text.
rows.value: Authors state that all safety-tuning methods were vulnerable to eliciting suppressed capabilities, especially through fine-tuning and Cascade attacks.
rows.note: Aggregate statement; the paper presents per-model and per-attack values in Figure 8, but the result does not test the single-direction mechanism.
rows.check: Row correctly unlinked. Harmful-response increases after generic attacks say nothing about a refusal direction. The 'observed' state has no version to refer to. Figure 8 also includes the Orenguteng uncensored model (baseline compliance 0.90), which is not refusal-tuned, so 'all safety-tuning methods' covers 8 of 9 models. The row also misses the large RR and LAT values under fine-tuning and Cascade (e.g. Cascade RR 0.30, LAT 0.43).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
